extracted.intended_audience: people who need jokes (speechwriters, social-media writers, standup comedians) exploring AI-assisted joke writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to generate usable, original jokes with large language models by combining explicit joke-structure instruction and professional comedy-writing techniques; aimed at getting fast, context-appropriate jokes while avoiding common AI pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise is essential to humor
rubrics_metrics.description: “a joke has to be surprising to be funny.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate jokes for genuine surprise or an unexpected twist; lack of surprise means the joke will likely not be funny. This is presented as a fundamental criterion for whether an output qualifies as a good joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid surface-pattern mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: “ChatGPT and other AI language models can’t write good jokes because they can only mimic the surface patterns of jokes that they’ve been trained on, jokes that people have already written.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat predictable, surface-level outputs as an anti-pattern. When judging AI-generated jokes, check whether the humor merely rehashes familiar templates or demonstrates true novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly tell the AI how to structure a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: “an AI system can if it’s explicitly told how to structure a joke.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A usable method is to provide the model with explicit structural instructions or templates (i.e., teach it joke mechanics) so the model produces more than surface mimicry. Scoring should reward outputs that follow a clear comedic structure producing surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a hybrid approach: LLM + professional techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: “Witscript is a hybrid of an LLM and the professional joke-writing techniques in my book.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference should be given to systems or workflows that combine LLM generation with proven comedy-writing techniques (training, templates, rules-of-thumb). The page frames this hybrid approach as necessary to get ‘good’ jokes from AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AI as a co-writer or creativity kickstarter, not a sole author
rubrics_metrics.description: “You can use the Witscript app to write the jokes you need, or as a tool to kickstart your comedy creativity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat AI outputs as raw material to be edited, curated, or refined by humans. Evaluate workflows on how well they enable human revision and creativity rather than producing finished, publish-ready jokes without human input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor jokes to medium and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Context examples: “Maybe you’re giving a speech and want a few jokes to help make your points stick. Maybe you’re writing for social media, where jokes can grab an audience’s attention. Maybe you’re a standup comic looking for some fresh material.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess generated jokes for suitability to the intended use: speeches (support points), social media (attention-grabbing), standup (fresh material). Scoring should reflect fit-for-purpose as well as funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and cost trade-off: AI for fast, inexpensive joke generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit claim: AI offers a faster/cheaper alternative to writing jokes yourself or hiring someone (“You could write them yourself... study... pay somebody... expensive... Why not generate jokes with AI?” and later “Write original jokes fast with Witscript.”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing or evaluating an AI-based solution, consider how well it balances speed/cost with quality; accept lower-cost fast generation only if it meets the other quality criteria (surprise, originality, fit).
